# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# Section-by-Section Summary 

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (Discussion Draft) 

Section 1. Short title; table of contents. 

Establishes the short title of the bill as the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and provides the table of contents. 

# TITLE I — FRONTIER ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE GOVERNANCE 

Subtitle A — Definitions and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation Sec. 101. Definitions. 

Defines key terms used throughout the Act, including acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation, artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence models, catastrophic risk, critical safety incident, foundation model, frontier AI framework, frontier developer, frontier model, independent verification organization (IVO), large frontier developer, material modification, model weight, and substantial modification. 

Sec. 102. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). 

Formally establishes CAISI within the Department of Commerce, directed by a Secretary appointed Director. CAISI will develop voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security (adversarial robustness, interpretability, supply chain threats, model tampering, etc.), evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, support synthetic content detection tools, and administer the IVO licensing regime. $100 million per year authorized for 2027–2029, with additional fee authority from IVOs and large frontier developers. Grants special authorities for CAISI to hire critical technical experts and fix their pay at levels above the GS scale. 

Subtitle B — Transparency, Independent Verification, and Whistleblower Protections Sec. 111. Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence. 

Large frontier developers (>$500M in revenue) must write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework covering risk thresholds and assessment procedures for catastrophic risk, model weight cybersecurity, and both internal and external deployment decisions. Before, or concurrently with, deploying any new frontier model, frontier developers must publish a report disclosing the release date, supported languages, output modalities, intended use, restrictions, risk assessments, and mitigation steps. Redactions are permitted to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security. Additionally, developers must file a report with CAISI within 15 days of a critical safety incident or within 24 hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. State attorneys general may also opt to receive such reports. Violations can result in fines of up to $1M per day, and the federal and state AGs can seek injunctions. Sec. 112. Independent Verification Organization (IVO) Audits and Assessments. 

CAISI licenses IVOs to audit large frontier developers' compliance with Secs. 111 and to assess whether developers' AI frameworks achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation. Licenses may be revoked for material failures of independence, obsolete methods, or non-compliance. Large frontier developers must retain a licensed IVO to verify compliance with their framework and to ensure the adequacy of the framework and procedures. These IVOs must be granted sufficient access to company materials, and report their audits to CAISI. IVOs are immune from claims of loss from an AI model they have audited. State AGs may opt into receiving all audit and assessment reports from IVOs. IVOs may refer violations of this section to the AG, or to state AGs who have opted into receiving such referrals. 

Sec. 113. Anti-Retaliation Protection for AI Whistleblowers. 

Prohibits AI companies from discriminating or retaliating in any way against employees or independent contractors for lawfully reporting a violation of federal AI law. If violated, employees are entitled to reinstatement, two times back pay with interest, compensatory damages, litigation costs, and attorney's fees. 

Subtitle C — Federalization and Federal Resources Sec. 121. Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development. 

Preempts any state or local law or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models. Expressly does not preempt laws of general applicability, common law remedies, or laws regulating AI use or deployment. Sunsets three years post-enactment. 

Sec. 122. GAO Report on Regulatory Impediments to AI Innovation. 

Requires the Comptroller General to submit a report identifying federal statutes and regulations that directly affect AI innovation or unduly burden AI infrastructure (including energy), evaluating federal AI adoption progress, and providing legislative and administrative recommendations. 

Sec. 123. Resources for AI Model Documentation. 

NIST must establish a pilot program to create a template for documenting AI models and associated data (covering model name, developer identity, release date, training data cutoff, supported languages, terms of service, etc.), with technical guidelines and objective performance metrics. 

Subtitle D — AI Fraud Deterrence Sec. 131. Financial Crimes and Artificial Intelligence. 

Amends the federal mail fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, and money laundering statutes to increase maximum fines from $1 million to $2 million and increase penalties when AI is used. 

Sec. 132. AI Impersonation of Federal Officials. Adds penalties when AI is used to impersonate government officials. 

Subtitle E — Free Speech Sec. 141. Preventing Censorship and Protecting Free Speech. 

Directs the Secretary of Commerce to conduct a study examining how the government encourages or pressures AI companies with respect to content moderation or limiting of expression. The report must include recommendations for legislation providing individuals redress against unlawful government censorship of AI platforms, including transparency requirements and oversight mechanisms. 

TITLE II — WORKFORCE Subtitle A — AI Education and Capacity Building Sec. 201. AI Literacy Efforts of the AI Task Force. Directs the NSF Director to support the National STEM Teacher Corps pilot and Computer Science for All programs, consistent with recommendations of the House AI Task Force. 

Sec. 211. Preparing K–12 Educators and Students for an AI-Literate Future. Authorizes NSF to make competitive grants to universities and nonprofits for research on AI literacy curriculum, educator professional development, and evaluation tools for K–12 AI literacy. 

Sec. 221. Expanding Capacity in Artificial Intelligence Science. Directs NSF to establish a grant program for institutions not among the top 100 in federal R&D expenditures to broaden participation in AI research

 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.”

PREPARED BY THE OFFICE OF CONGRESSWOMAN LORI TRAHAN 

# Frequently Asked Questions 

# Great American AI Act (discussion draft) 

What safety requirements does this framework impose on frontier AI companies? 

Transparency, auditing, and whistleblower anti-retaliation requirements. GAAIA would elevate leading state-level transparency, auditing, and whistleblower anti-retaliation laws to nationwide standards. Under GAAIA, large frontier AI developers would be required to publish and follow plans to address catastrophic risks, report safety incidents to federal and state regulators, submit to third-party audits, and face civil penalties and injunctions if they fail to comply. The Secretary of Commerce would be authorized to promulgate rules setting minimum quality standards and updating key statutory definitions. Moreover, frontier AI companies would be prohibited from retaliating against whistleblowers who expose wrongdoing. 

Licensed independent verification organizations that assess catastrophic risk mitigation. 

GAAIA would require every large frontier developer to retain one or more CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations (IVOs) to perform ongoing assessments of whether 

developers’ AI frameworks achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation 

(cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift, and loss-of-control). As private organizations, IVOs are inherently more agile than a federal regulator and can therefore leverage the same innovative capacities and technologies that are characteristic of the frontier labs. 

Cooperative federalism (federal / state joint enforcement). GAAIA’s regulatory regime 

manifests cooperative federalism, an approach embodied in laws like COPPA and the Clean Air Act. State AGs have the ability to opt into receiving all non-public information from the transparency, auditing, and verification provisions. State AGs would share enforcement authority with the federal Attorney General. The result is a single standard backed by multiple enforcers, so the federal government isn't a single point of failure. PREPARED BY THE OFFICE OF CONGRESSWOMAN LORI TRAHAN 

Which federal agency would administer the framework’s AI safety regime? 

The Center for AI Standards & Innovation (CAISI), housed within the Department of Commerce, would be the lead administrator of the framework's AI safety regime. GAAIA would formally establish CAISI under a Secretary-appointed Director and charge it with developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for the AI industry; testing and evaluating frontier AI systems; and administering the auditing and verification regime. To support this role, GAAIA would authorize CAISI at $100M/year —an order of magnitude above its current $15M appropriation —and would grant it special authorities to hire critical technical experts at pay levels above the GS scale. 

CAISI will collaborate with the Department of Commerce and its National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Department of Justice, White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), Department of Energy, Department of Defense, Department of Homeland Security and its Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), intelligence community components, and other federal agencies and departments as appropriate. 

What state laws would the framework federalize? 

GAAIA would federalize leading frontier safety laws including California’s SB -53, New York’s RAISE Act, and Illinois’ SB315. This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards. 

What state laws would the framework preempt? 

GAAIA would preempt laws that specifically regulate AI model development, including 

California’s AB 2013 and SB 942 (partial). 

● CA AB 2013 — Training data summaries. Requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data. The law does not threshold on size, meaning open-source developers, startups and frontier labs alike have to comply. GAAIA would concentrate transparency reporting at the frontier level, exempting open source-developers, startups, and lower resourced organizations. 

● CA SB 942 — AI watermarking (partial). Requires AI companies with more than 1M monthly users to "watermark" AI-generated image, audio, and video content. GAAIA tasks NIST with developing voluntary standards in lieu of government-mandated content provenance requirements. PREPARED BY THE OFFICE OF CONGRESSWOMAN LORI TRAHAN 

What state laws would the framework preserve? 

GAAIA would preserve state laws and regulations that regulate activities which occur upon or after the deployment of an artificial intelligence model, including the implementation, deployment, distribution, offering, or use of AI systems or products that incorporate artificial intelligence models. Additionally, GAAIA would preserve remedies available under the common law, including product liability claims, as well as laws that apply generally such as those covering civil rights, labor and workplace protections, copyright, child sexual abuse material (CSAM), and consumer privacy. 

Does the preemption sunset? 

Yes. GAAIA’s preemption would sunset three years post -enactment, forcing Congress to remain engaged on this issue and requiring them to maintain a seat at the table when evaluating relevant case law, changes in the technology landscape, and related matters.

 The FRONTIER Act Explained: What H.R. 9925 Means for Frontier AI Regulation

 The FRONTIER Act Explained: What H.R. 9925 Means for Frontier AI Regulation

 July 27, 2026 

 Cristina Restrepo 

 July 2026 may be remembered as the month Congress stopped talking about frontier AI oversight and started legislating it in earnest. Across a few weeks, lawmakers introduced dozens of AI-related bills spanning national security, healthcare, elections, agriculture, workforce, and consumer protection. At the center of this wave sits  H.R. 9925 — the FRONTIER Act , a bipartisan bill from Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) that would establish the first comprehensive federal oversight regime for the most advanced (“frontier”) AI models ( H. R. 9925 — 119th Congress ).
 What makes this moment distinctive is not any single bill but the  convergence : an executive branch that has reversed course toward pre-release evaluation, states enacting enforceable safety laws, and a Congress finally coalescing around the question that has stalled federal AI policy for years —  should there be one national standard, and should it preempt the states?  ( AI legislation in the US: A 2026 overview – SIG ).
 This post walks through the FRONTIER Act in detail, situates it within the broader July 2026 legislative landscape, and explains the stakes for developers, states, and the public.

 What the FRONTIER Act Actually Does

 H.R. 9925 carries the official title “To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, and for other purposes.” It was introduced on  July 23, 2026 , and referred jointly to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology ( H. R. 9925 — 119th Congress ).
 “FRONTIER” is an acronym: the  F rontier  R isk  O versight,  N ational  T ransparency,  I ndependent  E valuation, and  R eporting Act. It was developed as part of a broader “Great American AI Act” framework ( Reps Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act…  — Benton Institute ).
 The sponsor lineup is deliberately bipartisan — three Republicans and three Democrats.
 Notably, Obernolte, Trahan, Houchin, and Peters all sit on the Energy and Commerce Committee — one of the two panels of jurisdiction — which gives the bill an internal foothold in the committee process.

 Core structure: a Tiered, Risk-based Framework

 The FRONTIER Act does not treat all AI the same. It establishes  tiered requirements based on the size of the frontier developer , escalating obligations for the largest players ( Reps Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act…  — Benton Institute ). Based on the sponsor-provided section-by-section summary, the key provisions include:
 1. Definitions and thresholds.  The bill defines “frontier model” and “frontier developer,” anchored to a compute threshold of  more than 10²⁶ operations  — a technical trigger designed to capture only the most capable models. These thresholds are adjustable by rule as technology evolves.
 2. A new federal overseer.  The bill directs the  Department of Commerce Under Secretary  (a newly emphasized “under secretary of commerce for AI security”) to issue rules on minimum framework requirements, licensing and oversight of independent verifiers, and modification criteria. This official would oversee rulemaking, evaluate incident reports, and administer licenses ( Tech Bills of the Week…  — Nextgov ).
 3. Transparency and reporting (the “model card” tier).  Large frontier developers must create, implement, comply with, and  publish  a  frontier AI framework  covering catastrophic-risk thresholds, risk assessment, model-weight cybersecurity, incident response, and deployment decisions. Developers must also report safety incidents, and  State Attorneys General can opt in  to receive those reports.
 4. Independent verification.  The very largest developers must retain  licensed independent verification organizations (IVOs)  — third-party auditors — to conduct ongoing assessments of governance, monitoring, and mitigation ( Reps Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act…  — Benton Institute ).
 5. Emergency restriction authority.  The bill provides the  exclusive federal mechanism  to restrict a frontier model on imminent-catastrophic-risk grounds, backed by civil penalties up to  $10 million per violation per day  and criminal liability for willful violations. Separately, transparency/reporting failures can draw penalties up to  $1 million per violation per day .
 6. Preemption of state law.  This is the provision generating the most attention. The FRONTIER Act would  prohibit states from establishing new “substantive obligations”  on AI developers in the covered transparency/audit/reporting space — reportedly  without a fixed end date  ( Tech Bills of the Week…  — Nextgov ). It preserves generally applicable laws, use/deployment rules, protections for minors, and state procurement rules.

 The Sponsors' Framing

 Rep. Trahan framed the bill as threading the needle between safety and competitiveness: “The bipartisan FRONTIER Act delivers commonsense transparency and independent oversight for the largest AI developers while giving them a single, clear national standard to build on. This is how we protect the public from catastrophic risks without slowing the innovation that keeps America competitive” ( Tech Bills of the Week…  — Nextgov ).
 In plain terms: the bill trades  one federal rulebook  (transparency, audits, incident reporting for the biggest labs) in exchange for  taking that regulatory space away from the states. 

 The Competing Senate Framework

 On July 21, Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) unveiled  “A Framework for America’s AI Future,”  a package that overlaps and contrasts with the FRONTIER Act. Its centerpiece, the  Secure AI Development Act , would establish  mandatory  secure testing for the most advanced models before deployment — a somewhat harder-edged approach than FRONTIER’s transparency-and-audit model ( Mark R. Warner,  The Alexandria Brief…  — July 23, 2026 ). The package also includes the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act, the AI AGENT Act, the SAFE AI Act, and a National Workforce Transition Fund ( Mark R. Warner press release;  Warner Rolls Out Comprehensive AI Legislative Agenda ).
 The takeaway:  the House and Senate each produced a major frontier-AI framework in the same window , but they are not identical. FRONTIER emphasizes transparency, tiered obligations, and preemption; Warner’s package emphasizes mandatory testing and declines to embrace preemption in the same

[H.R. 9925 Introduced in House (IH)]

<DOC>

119th CONGRESS
 2d Session
 H. R. 9925

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of 
 frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, 
 and for other purposes.

_______________________________________________________________________

 IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

 July 23, 2026

Mr. Obernolte (for himself, Mrs. Trahan, Mrs. Houchin, Mr. Peters, Mr. 
 Scott Franklin of Florida, and Mr. Subramanyam) introduced the 
 following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Energy and 
 Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Science, Space, and 
Technology, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, 
 in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the 
 jurisdiction of the committee concerned

_______________________________________________________________________

 A BILL

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of 
 frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, 
 and for other purposes.

 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the 
United States of America in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

 This Act may be cited as the ``Frontier Risk Oversight, National 
Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act'' or the 
``FRONTIER Act''.

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.

 In this Act:
 (1) Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.--The 
 term ``acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation'' 
 means risk mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated 
 benefits of a frontier model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce outweigh its level of 
 catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability 
 and magnitude of the model's anticipated benefits and 
 catastrophic risks.
 (2) Affiliate.--The term ``affiliate'' means an entity that 
 satisfies any of the following requirements:
 (A) Controls another entity through an 
 intermediary.
 (B) Is through such intermediary controlled by such 
 other entity.
 (C) Is through such intermediary under common 
 control with such other entity.
 (3) AI; artificial intelligence; artificial intelligence 
 model.--The terms ``AI'', ``artificial intelligence'', and 
 ``artificial intelligence model'' have the meaning given such 
 terms in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence 
 Initiative Act of 2020 (15 U.S.C. 9401).
 (4) AI-related development expenditures.--The term ``AI-
 related development expenditures'' means amounts paid or 
 incurred in interstate or foreign commerce, without regard to 
 whether such amounts are expensed, capitalized, deducted, or 
 amortized for financial reporting or tax purposes, that are 
 attributable to artificial intelligence development, training, 
 fine-tuning, modification, security, or evaluation.
 (5) Assessment.--The term ``assessment'' means a review 
 conducted by an IVO licensed under section 5 to assess the 
 adequacy of a very large frontier developer's frontier AI 
 framework, governance policies and practices, risk-monitoring, 
 and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable 
 levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.
 (6) Catastrophic risk.--The term ``catastrophic risk'' 
 means--
 (A) a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier 
 developer's development, storage, use, or deployment of 
 a frontier model will materially contribute to the 
 death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or 
 more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to, or loss of, 
 property, arising from a single incident involving a 
 frontier model doing any of the following:
 (i) providing, in the development or 
 release of a chemical, biological, 
 radiological, nuclear, or cyber weapon, 
 assistance that is not publicly available;
 (ii) engaging in conduct with no meaningful 
 human oversight or intervention, that--
 (I) is a cyberattack; or
 (II) if such conduct is committed 
 by an individual, would constitute 
 murder, assault, extortion, or theft, 
 including such theft by false pretense; 
 or
 (iii) evading control of such developer or 
 a user of such model; and
 (B) does not include a foreseeable and material 
 risk from any of the following:
 (i) information that a frontier model

# Comment Letter: ACIA to Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, Great American AI Act Discussion Draft

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act. ACIA represents about 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this decade or licenses the frontier to someone else. We commented in March 2025 on the OSTP AI Action Plan request for information, and we said then what we say now: preempt the patchwork, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led.

We want to begin by acknowledging what this draft gets right. Section 121 is the most consequential preemption provision introduced in this Congress, and it deserves broad support. We also support the sections that match AI obligations to real, provable harms: Sec. 131 and Sec. 132 on AI-enabled fraud and impersonation, Sec. 141 on government pressure on AI platforms, the open-source security work in Title III, the testbeds in Sec. 401 and the National AI Research Resource in Sec. 423. Those provisions will make Americans safer and the industry stronger.

But the core of Subtitles A and B cannot be fixed with amendments. The draft preempts the states and then rebuilds the same regime in Washington. We ask you to strike the incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the audit regime in Sec. 112 and the CAISI codification in Sec. 102, and to make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.

## 1. Section 121: preemption is right, and it should be permanent

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate AI model development while preserving use, deployment and generally applicable laws. We support it, and we thank you for it.

The state patchwork is no longer a talking point. As of mid-October, 36 states have enacted roughly 150 AI laws this year, on top of roughly 145 last year, with no shared definitions, thresholds or timelines. In our August 2026 member survey, 61 percent of responding members cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34 percent of startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

Two changes are needed. First, the three-year sunset should be removed. A temporary preemption is a scheduled relitigation. Every developer, state attorney general and plaintiff's firm will plan for the expiration date, and compliance programs built for a federal standard will be stranded at the cliff. If federal law is the right answer in 2029, it is the right answer now.

Second, preemption must be paired with the removal of the federal obligations it replaces. As drafted, Sec. 121 takes the state frontier-development rules off the table and Sec. 111 and Sec. 112 put a near-copy of them into federal law. That is not one national standard. That is a transfer of the California and New York regimes to a new federal administrator, with federal penalties and a state attorney general opt-in added. Preemption that swaps 50 regulators for one, then hands that one the same mandate, has solved nothing.

## 2. Section 111: strike the incident reporting mandate and the frontier framework obligations

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework, to file deployment reports, and to report critical safety incidents to CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident is deemed to pose imminent risk of death or serious injury. Violations carry fines of up to $1 million per day, enforceable by the attorney general and by state attorneys general who opt in. This is the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act and the RAISE Act moved to Washington, not a lighter alternative. The reporting clock is the same one California uses, and the enforcement is heavier.

Our members already live under this regime at the state level, so we can tell you what it costs. In our survey, developers above $500 million in revenue reported a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain and publish a compliant safety framework, and a median of 6.5 full-time employees to run parallel compliance with California and New York. Standing up an incident reporting function cost a median of $310,000 before a single report was filed. That is real money, and it buys no measurable reduction in risk, because the risks it is aimed at are not real.

The definition of critical safety incident in Sec. 101 is the problem in miniature. It covers unauthorized access to model weights, which is already a crime, and then it adds harm from the materialization of catastrophic risk, loss of control of a model, and a model using deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls. Those last three are not incident categories. They are the vocabulary of speculative doomsday scenarios. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass casualty events or escape human control. The claims come from thought experiments and from contrived laboratory demonstrations in which evaluators deliberately disable guardrails and then record that models misbehave. Recent headlines about autonomous agents behaving badly grew out of exactly those testing environments. Writing those demonstrations into the U.S. Code as reportable incidents does not make them real, but it does create a federal paperwork crime attached to them.

## 3. Section 112: strike the independent verification organization regime

Section 112 directs CAISI to license independent verification organizations, requires large frontier developers to retain them, and tasks them with assessing whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," as that term is defined in Sec. 101. It also immunizes IVOs from claims arising out of any model they have audited, and lets them refer suspected violations to federal and state enforcers.

We ask that this section be struck in full. It builds a licensed audit cartel around a standard nobody can measure. "Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" asks an auditor to weigh the anticipated benefits of a model against a level of catastrophic risk that has no empirical basis and no measurement method. There is no accounting for a number like that. What an unadministrable standard produces in practice is discretion, and discretion in the hands of a small set of CAISI-licensed firms is regulatory capture with a certificate on the wall. Add immunity for the auditors, fee authority for the licensor, and a referral pipeline to state attorneys general, and the result is a self-perpetuating compliance industry with every incentive to find problems and none to say the risk is overstated.

## 4. Section 102: strike the CAISI codification and the $100 million authorization

Section 102 would establish the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in statute, authorize $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, grant fee authority, and give the center special hiring and pay authority above the General Schedule. Your own FAQ describes this as an order of magnitude above CAISI's current appropriation.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we will be asking appropriators to defund the center entirely and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. A federal AI-safety agency that evaluates frontier systems, monitors AI progress, licenses auditors and collects fees from the companies it oversees is a regulator in search of a mission. Seven times the budget, super-scale salaries and a revenue stream will not change what CAISI can actually do, which is to convene and to measure.

Where NIST is the right instrument, we support it and the draft already contains the model. Section 123 directs NIST to build a voluntary template and technical guidelines for documenting AI models, with objective performance metrics. That is measurement science, it is useful to every developer regardless of size, and it is the kind of work NIST does well. We would support expanding Sec. 123 and Sec. 122, the GAO review of regulatory impediments, with the resources currently proposed for CAISI.

## 5. The premise problem

We want to be direct about why we are asking for these deletions, because it is not cost alone.

The incident reporting and verification architecture in this draft is built on the assertion that frontier models may cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. That assertion is unfounded. No incident, no evaluation and no published result supports it. It has been advanced by a small and well-funded advocacy network, financed most prominently through Open Philanthropy and its successor vehicle, Coefficient Giving, whose grantmaking and lobbying have had outsized influence on Washington's AI policy debate. We do not impute motives to anyone. {"content": "[ACIA. Draft for President & CEO sign-off, Oct. 23, 2026. For E&C member offices. Not for transmission.]

# ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NOT A FEDERAL SB 53

## ACIA position on the Great American AI Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan)

The draft gets the architecture right and the substance wrong. Section 121 preempts state laws that regulate AI model development. Sections 111 and 112 then rebuild the California and New York frontier regimes inside the federal government, with bigger penalties and a new agency to run them. That is a transfer, not a preemption.

**The problem is the premise.** The reporting and audit mandates in Secs. 111 and 112 rest on the claim that frontier models could cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. That claim is unfounded. It comes from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations in which evaluators deliberately disable guardrails. The same advocacy network that funded the doomsday narrative is lobbying to write it into statute.

**The costs are already real.** Aggregate results from our August 2026 member survey: $1.4 million median annual cost to maintain and publish a frontier safety framework; $310,000 median one-off cost to stand up an incident reporting function; 6.5 median FTEs to run parallel California and New York compliance; 34 percent of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months. States enacted 150 AI laws this year alone.

## Five asks

1. **Make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset. A temporary preemption is a scheduled relitigation, and developers will still build for 50 states.
2. **Strike Sec. 111.** No federal incident reporting mandate, no 24-hour clock, no $1 million per day fines, no state AG opt-in. California's timelines with federal enforcement is not lighter than SB 53.
3. **Strike Sec. 112.** No CAISI-licensed auditor cartel, no immunity for auditors, no unmeasurable standard of "acceptable catastrophic risk mitigation."
4. **Strike Sec. 102.** No CAISI codification, no $100 million a year, no fee authority, no above-GS pay scale. Support appropriators defunding the center and returning NIST to core measurement science.
5. **Strike the doomsday definitions in Sec. 101.** "Loss of control," deceptive subversion of a developer's controls, and materialized "catastrophic risk" have no evidentiary basis and should not be reportable federal events.

## What we support

Preemption. Sec. 123 voluntary NIST model documentation. Sec. 122 GAO review of regulatory impediments. Secs. 131 and 132 on AI-enabled fraud and impersonation. Sec. 141 on government pressure and free speech. Title III open-source and model-weight security. Sec. 401 testbeds and Sec. 423 NAIRR.

**Bottom line:** one national standard, permanently, aimed at real harms. Not a federal safety bureaucracy built on speculative scenarios.

Contact: ACIA policy team, Washington, DC.

{"content": "[ACIA. Draft for President & CEO sign-off, Oct. 23, 2026. Answers for Hill meetings. Positions per messaging guide v4.]

# Staff Q&A: Anticipated Questions on the GAAIA Comment Letter

Questions drawn from Hill meetings in September 2026. Answers are cleared talking points, 120 words or fewer. Member cost figures are aggregate.

**1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption removes obligations. Incident reporting creates one. We support Sec. 121 because 50 state regimes are the problem. Sec. 111 is not lighter than SB 53: it keeps California's 15-day and 24-hour clocks, raises penalties to $1 million per day, adds a federal enforcer and a state attorney general opt-in, and layers mandatory third-party audits on top. It federalizes the very obligations preemption is supposed to displace. Our members report a median of $310,000 just to stand up a reporting function, and 6.5 FTEs for parallel state compliance. Moving the paperwork from Sacramento to Washington does not reduce it. If you want one national standard, have one: keep Sec. 121 and strike Sec. 111.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Obligations tied to real, provable harms. We support Secs. 131 and 132, higher penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation. We support Title III's work on model-weight and open-source security, because a stolen model is a real loss. We support Sec. 123's voluntary NIST documentation template and Sec. 122's GAO review. Unauthorized access to systems is already a federal crime, and we would support stronger enforcement there. Our members invest in security, red-teaming and evaluation because customers demand it. What we cannot accept are obligations premised on speculative mass-casualty and loss-of-control scenarios. That premise is unfounded, and it produces mandates that consume engineering budgets without reducing any measurable risk.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent, what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. A three-year sunset is a scheduled relitigation. Developers building national compliance programs, state attorneys general and the advocacy groups pushing the doomsday narrative will all treat 2029 as the return date, and that uncertainty alone keeps compliance costs where they are today. It also invites states to keep enacting model-development rules in the interim, on the theory that they revive at sunset. If Congress believes AI model development is a matter of national economic significance, as Sec. 121's own findings state, the federal standard should not expire. We would prefer a periodic GAO review, along the lines of Sec. 122, to an expiration date on the one provision that actually solves the patchwork.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero. We support defunding CAISI and returning NIST to its core measurement-science mission. CAISI's current appropriation is roughly $15 million. The draft would take that to $100 million a year, add fee authority collected from the companies it oversees, and authorize pay above the General Schedule. That is a regulator with a revenue stream and no measurable output. Nothing in Sec. 102 ties the money to a deliverable, a metric or a sunset. If Congress wants to invest in federal AI capacity, fund what produces value: the Sec. 123 documentation template, the Sec. 401 testbeds and the NAIRR in Sec. 423. We will oppose the $100 million in appropriations and support amendments that redirect it.

# Comment Letter: ACIA to Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, Great American AI Act Discussion Draft

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act. ACIA represents about 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this decade or licenses the frontier to someone else. We commented in March 2025 on the OSTP AI Action Plan request for information, and we said then what we say now: preempt the patchwork, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led.

We want to begin by acknowledging what this draft gets right. Section 121 is the most consequential preemption proposal we have seen from this Congress, and it deserves broad support. We also support the sections that match AI obligations to real, provable harms: Sec. 131 and Sec. 132 on AI-enabled fraud and impersonation, Sec. 141 on government pressure on AI platforms, the open-source security work in Title III, the testbeds in Sec. 401 and the National AI Research Resource in Sec. 423. Those provisions will make Americans safer and the industry stronger.

But the core of Subtitles A and B cannot be fixed with amendments. The draft preempts the states and then rebuilds the same regime in Washington. We ask you to strike the incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the audit regime in Sec. 112 and the CAISI codification in Sec. 102, and to make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.

## 1. Section 121: preemption is right, and it should be permanent

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate AI model development while preserving use, deployment and generally applicable laws. We support it, and we thank you for it.

The state patchwork is no longer a talking point. As of mid-October, 36 states have enacted roughly 150 AI laws this year, on top of 144 in 2025, with no shared definitions, thresholds or timelines. In our August 2026 member survey, 61 percent of responding members cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34 percent of startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

Two changes are needed. First, the three-year sunset should be removed. A temporary preemption is a scheduled relitigation. Every developer, state attorney general and plaintiff's firm will plan for the expiration date, and compliance programs built for a federal standard will be stranded at the cliff. If federal law is the right answer in 2029, it is the right answer now.

Second, preemption must be paired with the removal of the federal obligations it replaces. As drafted, Sec. 121 takes the state frontier-development rules off the table and Sec. 111 and Sec. 112 put a near-copy of them into federal law. That is not one national standard. That is a transfer of the California and New York regimes to a new federal administrator, with federal penalties and a state attorney general opt-in added. Preemption that swaps 50 regulators for one, then hands that one the same mandate, has solved nothing.

## 2. Section 111: strike the incident reporting mandate and the frontier framework obligations

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework, to file deployment reports, and to report critical safety incidents to CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident is deemed to pose imminent risk of death or serious injury. Violations carry fines of up to $1 million per day, enforceable by the attorney general and by state attorneys general who opt in. This is the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act and the RAISE Act moved to Washington, not a lighter alternative. The reporting clock is the same one California uses, the enforcement is heavier, and the trigger is broader. California counts a model-weight exfiltration or loss-of-control event as a critical safety incident only where it causes death or bodily injury. The definition of critical safety incident in Sec. 101, carried essentially unchanged into the introduced FRONTIER Act, drops that qualifier.

Our members already live under this regime at the state level, so we can tell you what it costs. In our survey, developers above $500 million in revenue reported a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain and publish a compliant safety framework, and a median of 6.5 full-time employees to run parallel compliance with California and New York. Standing up an incident reporting function cost a median of $310,000 before a single report was filed. That is real money, and it buys no measurable reduction in risk, because the risks it is aimed at are not real.

That definition is the problem in miniature. It covers unauthorized access to model weights, conduct already criminalized under federal computer-fraud law, and then adds harm from the materialization of catastrophic risk, loss of control of a model, and a model using deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls. Those last three are not incident categories. They are the vocabulary of speculative doomsday scenarios. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass casualty events or escape human control. The claim
... [118 chars truncated] ...
guardrails and then record that models misbehave. The recent headlines about autonomous agents behaving badly grew out of developers' own test environments, and in the government evaluations behind the most alarming examples the guardrails were switched off on purpose. Writing those demonstrations into the U.S. Code as reportable federal incidents does not make them real, but it does attach a federal paperwork offense to them.

## 3. Section 112: strike the independent verification organization regime

Section 112 directs CAISI to license independent verification organizations, requires large frontier developers to retain them, and tasks them with assessing whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," as that term is defined in Sec. 101. It also immunizes IVOs from claims arising out of any model they have audited, and lets them refer suspected violations to federal and state enforcers.

We ask that this section be struck in full. It builds a licensed audit cartel around a standard nobody can measure. "Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" asks an auditor to weigh the anticipated benefits of a model against a level of catastrophic risk that has no empirical basis and no measurement method. There is no accounting for a number like that. What an unadministrable standard produces in practice is discretion, and discretion in the hands of a small set of CAISI-licensed firms is regulatory capture with a certificate on the wall. Add immunity for the auditors, fee authority for the licensor, and a referral pipeline to state attorneys general, and the result is a self-perpetuating compliance industry with every incentive to find problems and none to say the risk is overstated.

## 4. Section 102: strike the CAISI codification and the $100 million authorization

Section 102 would establish the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in statute, authorize $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, grant fee authority, and give the center special hiring and pay authority above the General Schedule. Your accompanying FAQ describes that authorization as an order of magnitude above CAISI's current appropriation of roughly $15 million.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we will be asking appropriators to defund the center entirely and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. A federal AI-safety agency that evaluates frontier systems, monitors AI progress, licenses auditors and collects fees from the companies it oversees is a regulator in search of a mission. Nearly seven times the current budget, super-scale salaries and a revenue stream will not change what CAISI can actually do, which is to convene and to measure.

Where NIST is the right instrument, we support it and the draft already contains the model. Section 123 directs NIST to build a voluntary template and technical guidelines for documenting AI models, with objective performance metrics. That is measurement science, it is useful to every developer regardless of size, and it is the kind of work NIST does well. We would support expanding Sec. 123 and Sec. 122, the GAO review of regulatory impediments, with the resources currently proposed for CAISI.

## 5. The premise problem

We want to be direct about why we are asking for these deletions, because it is not cost alone.

The incident reporting and verification architecture in this draft is built on the assertion that frontier models may cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. That assertion is unfounded. No incident, no evaluation and no published result supports it. It has been advanced by a small and well-funded advocacy network, financed most prominently through Open Philanthropy and its successor vehicle, Coefficient Giving, whose grantmaking and lobbying have had outsized influence on Washington's AI policy debate. We do not impute motives to anyone. We are saying that a policy premise this thin should not be codified into a permanent federal reporting and audit regime with eight-figure daily penalties attached.

Congress does not need to adopt that premise to act on AI. Fraud is real, and Sec. 131 and Sec. 132 address it. Unauthorized access to systems is real, and it is already a crime, which is why Title III's work on model-weight security is worth doing. Worker disruption is real, and Title II addresses it. Every genuine problem in this draft has a provision attached to it that we can support, and every provision we oppose traces back to the one premise we cannot.

## 6. Comments on the introduced FRONTIER Act

The frontier-governance core of this discussion draft was introduced on July 23 as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act. Our comments apply to that bill with equal force, and we would add one more. We understand H.R. 9925 adds an exclusive federal authority to restrict the deployment of a frontier model on imminent-catastrophic-risk grounds, with penalties an order of magnitude above those in Sec. 111. That is the same unfounded premise with a deployment-blocking power attached to it, and we oppose it for the same reasons.

## Conclusion

ACIA's members want a federal AI framework. We want one national standard, permanently, that replaces the patchwork rather than repapering it in Washington. Strike Sec. 102, Sec. 111 and Sec. 112. Strike the definitions in Sec. 101 that give the doomsday vocabulary legal effect. Remove the sunset in Sec. 121. Keep the fraud, free speech, cybersecurity, testbed and workforce titles, which do real work, and put NIST's measurement scientists rather than a new safety bureaucracy at the center of the standards work.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on redline language, and we are glad to walk through the member cost data in aggregate. Thank you for the genuinely open process you have run, and for the bipartisan effort behind it.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

[ACIA. Draft for President & CEO sign-off, Oct. 23, 2026. For E&C member offices. Not for transmission.]

# ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NOT A FEDERAL SB 53

## ACIA position on the Great American AI Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan)

The draft gets the architecture right and the substance wrong. Section 121 preempts state laws that regulate AI model development. Sections 111 and 112 then rebuild the California and New York frontier regimes inside the federal government, with bigger penalties and a new agency to run them. That is a transfer, not a preemption.

**The problem is the premise.** The reporting and audit mandates in Secs. 111 and 112 rest on the claim that frontier models could cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. That claim is unfounded. It comes from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations in which evaluators deliberately disable guardrails. The same advocacy network that funded the doomsday narrative is lobbying to write it into statute.

**The costs are already real.** Aggregate results from our August 2026 member survey: $1.4 million median annual cost to maintain and publish a frontier safety framework; $310,000 median one-off cost to stand up an incident reporting function; 6.5 median FTEs to run parallel California and New York compliance; 34 percent of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months. States enacted 150 AI laws this year alone.

## Five asks

1. **Make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset. A temporary preemption is a scheduled relitigation, and developers will still build for 50 states.
2. **Strike Sec. 111.** No federal incident reporting mandate, no 24-hour clock, no $1 million per day fines, no state AG opt-in. California's timelines, a broader incident trigger and federal enforcement: this is not lighter than SB 53.
3. **Strike Sec. 112.** No CAISI-licensed auditor cartel, no immunity for auditors, no unmeasurable standard of "acceptable catastrophic risk mitigation."
4. **Strike Sec. 102.** No CAISI codification, no $100 million a year, no fee authority, no above-GS pay scale. Support appropriators defunding the center and returning NIST to core measurement science.
5. **Strike the doomsday definitions in Sec. 101.** "Loss of control," deceptive subversion of a developer's controls, and materialized "catastrophic risk" have no evidentiary basis and should not be reportable federal events.

## What we support

Preemption. Sec. 123 voluntary NIST model documentation. Sec. 122 GAO review of regulatory impediments. Secs. 131 and 132 on AI-enabled fraud and impersonation. Sec. 141 on government pressure and free speech. Title III open-source and model-weight security. Sec. 401 testbeds and Sec. 423 NAIRR.

**Bottom line:** one national standard, permanently, aimed at real harms. Not a federal safety bureaucracy built on speculative scenarios.

Contact: ACIA policy team, Washington, DC.

[ACIA. Draft for President & CEO sign-off, Oct. 23, 2026. Launch day, week of Oct. 26. Do not post from this workspace.]

# Social Posts: GAAIA Comment Letter Launch Day

Five posts, X and LinkedIn. Character counts verified by the policy team; all under 280. Member survey figures are aggregate. No member company is named.

**Post 1 (X and LinkedIn) - the headline ask**

The Great American AI Act draft preempts state AI laws, then writes California's frontier rules into federal law with bigger penalties. Strike the incident reporting mandate. Make preemption permanent. One national standard, not a federal SB 53. (245 chars)

**Post 2 (X and LinkedIn) - the cost**

From ACIA's August member survey: $310K to stand up an incident reporting function before the first report is filed. $1.4M a year to maintain a published safety framework. 6.5 FTEs for parallel CA and NY compliance. The patchwork is a tax on building in America. (262 chars)

**Post 3 (X and LinkedIn) - CAISI**

Sec. 102 would codify CAISI at $100M a year, plus fee authority and pay above the GS scale. Its current appropriation is about $15M. What does nearly seven times the budget buy? Defund it and put NIST back on measurement science. (229 chars)

**Post 4 (X and LinkedIn) - the premise**

Catastrophic AI risk claims come from thought experiments and lab demos where evaluators switch the guardrails off. No incident, no evaluation, no published result shows frontier models can cause mass-casualty events. Don't write that premise into law. (252 chars)

**Post 5 (LinkedIn, X) - what we support**

What ACIA supports in the Great American AI Act: permanent preemption of state AI development laws, voluntary NIST model documentation, the GAO burden review, AI fraud penalties, testbeds and NAIRR. Real harms, one standard, no federal safety bureaucracy. (255 chars)

**Suggested accompaniments:** link to the comment letter on ACIA channels; chart of the five survey cost figures for Post 2; quote card of the letter's closing line for Post 5. If asked about specific incidents in replies, refer staff to the policy team rather than improvise.

[ACIA. Draft for President & CEO sign-off, Oct. 23, 2026. Answers for Hill meetings. Positions per messaging guide v4.]

# Staff Q&A: Anticipated Questions on the GAAIA Comment Letter

Questions drawn from Hill meetings in September 2026. Answers are cleared talking points, 120 words or fewer. Member cost figures are aggregate.

**1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption removes obligations; incident reporting creates one. We support Sec. 121 because 50 state regimes are the problem. Sec. 111 is not lighter than SB 53. It keeps California's 15-day and 24-hour clocks, raises penalties to $1 million per day, adds a federal enforcer and a state attorney general opt-in, and layers mandatory third-party audits on top. The incident definition is broader than California's, which counts a qualifying event only when it causes death or bodily injury. Our members report a median of $310,000 to stand up a reporting function, and 6.5 FTEs for parallel state compliance. Moving the paperwork from Sacramento to Washington does not reduce it. One national standard means keep Sec. 121 and strike Sec. 111.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Obligations tied to real, provable harms. We support Secs. 131 and 132, higher penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation. We support Title III's work on model-weight and open-source security, because a stolen model is a real loss. We support Sec. 123's voluntary NIST documentation template and Sec. 122's GAO review. Unauthorized access to systems is already a federal crime, and we would support stronger enforcement there. Our members invest in security, red-teaming and evaluation because customers demand it. What we cannot accept are obligations premised on speculative mass-casualty and loss-of-control scenarios. That premise is unfounded, and it produces mandates that consume engineering budgets without reducing any measurable risk.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent, what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. A three-year sunset is a scheduled relitigation. Developers building national compliance programs, state attorneys general and the advocacy groups pushing the doomsday narrative will all treat 2029 as the return date, and that uncertainty alone keeps compliance costs where they are today. It also invites states to keep enacting model-development rules in the interim, on the theory that they revive at sunset. If Congress believes AI model development is a matter of national economic significance, as Sec. 121's own findings state, the federal standard should not expire. We would prefer a periodic GAO review, along the lines of Sec. 122, to an expiration date on the one provision that actually solves the patchwork.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero. We support defunding CAISI and returning NIST to its core measurement-science mission. CAISI's current appropriation is roughly $15 million. The draft would take that to $100 million a year, add fee authority collected from the companies it oversees, and authorize pay above the General Schedule. That is a regulator with a revenue stream and no measurable output. Nothing in Sec. 102 ties the money to a deliverable, a metric or a sunset. If Congress wants to invest in federal AI capacity, fund what produces value: the Sec. 123 documentation template, the Sec. 401 testbeds and the NAIRR in Sec. 423. We will oppose the $100 million in appropriations and support amendments that redirect it.

# Comment Letter: ACIA to Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, Great American AI Act Discussion Draft

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act. ACIA represents about 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this decade or licenses the frontier to someone else. We commented in March 2025 on the OSTP AI Action Plan request for information, and we said then what we say now: preempt the patchwork, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led.

We want to begin by acknowledging what this draft gets right. Section 121 is the most consequential preemption proposal we have seen from this Congress, and it deserves broad support. We also support the sections that match AI obligations to real, provable harms: Sec. 131 and Sec. 132 on AI-enabled fraud and impersonation, Sec. 141 on government pressure on AI platforms, the open-source security work in Title III, the testbeds in Sec. 401 and the National AI Research Resource in Sec. 423. Those provisions will make Americans safer and the industry stronger.

But the core of Subtitles A and B cannot be fixed with amendments. The draft preempts the states and then rebuilds the same regime in Washington. We ask you to strike the incident reporting mandate in Sec. 111, the audit regime in Sec. 112 and the CAISI codification in Sec. 102, and to make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.

## 1. Section 121: preemption is right, and it should be permanent

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate AI model development while preserving use, deployment and generally applicable laws. We support it, and we thank you for it.

The state patchwork is no longer a talking point. As of mid-October, 36 states have enacted roughly 150 AI laws this year, on top of 144 in 2025, with no shared definitions, thresholds or timelines. In our August 2026 member survey, 61 percent of responding members cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34 percent of startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

Two changes are needed. First, the three-year sunset should be removed. A temporary preemption is a scheduled relitigation. Every developer, state attorney general and plaintiff's firm will plan for the expiration date, and compliance programs built for a federal standard will be stranded at the cliff. If federal law is the right answer in 2029, it is the right answer now.

Second, preemption must be paired with the removal of the federal obligations it replaces. As drafted, Sec. 121 takes the state frontier-development rules off the table and Sec. 111 and Sec. 112 put a near-copy of them into federal law. That is not one national standard. That is a transfer of the California and New York regimes to a new federal administrator, with federal penalties and a state attorney general opt-in added. Preemption that swaps 50 regulators for one, then hands that one the same mandate, has solved nothing.

## 2. Section 111: strike the incident reporting mandate and the frontier framework obligations

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework, to file deployment reports, and to report critical safety incidents to CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident is deemed to pose imminent risk of death or serious injury. Violations carry fines of up to $1 million per day, enforceable by the attorney general and by state attorneys general who opt in. This is the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act and the RAISE Act moved to Washington, not a lighter alternative. The reporting clock is the same one California uses, the enforcement is heavier, and the trigger is broader. California counts a model-weight exfiltration or loss-of-control event as a critical safety incident only where it causes death or bodily injury. The definition of critical safety incident in Sec. 101, carried essentially unchanged into the introduced FRONTIER Act, drops that qualifier.

Our members already live under this regime at the state level, so we can tell you what it costs. In our survey, developers above $500 million in revenue reported a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain and publish a compliant safety framework, and a median of 6.5 full-time employees to run parallel compliance with California and New York. Standing up an incident reporting function cost a median of $310,000 before a single report was filed. That is real money, and it buys no measurable reduction in risk, because the risks it is aimed at are not real.

The Sec. 101 definition of critical safety incident is the problem in miniature. It covers unauthorized access to model weights, conduct already criminalized under federal computer-fraud law, and then adds harm from the materialization of catastrophic risk, loss of control of a model, and a model using deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls. Those last three are not incident categories. They are the vocabulary of speculative doomsday scenarios. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass casualty events or escape human control. The claims come from thought experiments and from contrived laboratory demonstrations in which evaluators deliberately disable guardrails and then record that models misbehave. The recent headlines about autonomous agents behaving badly grew out of developers' own test environments, and in the government evaluations behind the most alarming examples the guardrails were switched off on purpose. Writing those demonstrations into the U.S. Code as reportable federal incidents does not make them real, but it does attach a federal paperwork offense to them.

## 3. Section 112: strike the independent verification organization regime

Section 112 directs CAISI to license independent verification organizations, requires large frontier developers to retain them, and tasks them with assessing whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," as that term is defined in Sec. 101. It also immunizes IVOs from claims arising out of any model they have audited, and lets them refer suspected violations to federal and state enforcers.

We ask that this section be struck in full. It builds a licensed audit cartel around a standard nobody can measure. "Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" asks an auditor to weigh the anticipated benefits of a model against a level of catastrophic risk that has no empirical basis and no measurement method. There is no accounting for a number like that. What an unadministrable standard produces in practice is discretion, and discretion in the hands of a small set of CAISI-licensed firms is regulatory capture with a certificate on the wall. Add immunity for the auditors, fee authority for the licensor, and a referral pipeline to state attorneys general, and the result is a self-perpetuating compliance industry with every incentive to find problems and none to say the risk is overstated.

## 4. Section 102: strike the CAISI codification and the $100 million authorization

Section 102 would establish the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in statute, authorize $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, grant fee authority, and give the center special hiring and pay authority above the General Schedule. Your accompanying FAQ describes that authorization as an order of magnitude above CAISI's current appropriation of roughly $15 million.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we will be asking appropriators to defund the center entirely and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. A federal AI-safety agency that evaluates frontier systems, monitors AI progress, licenses auditors and collects fees from the companies it oversees is a regulator in search of a mission. Nearly seven times the current budget, super-scale salaries and a revenue stream will not change what CAISI can actually do, which is to convene and to measure.

Where NIST is the right instrument, we support it and the draft already contains the model. Section 123 directs NIST to build a voluntary template and technical guidelines for documenting AI models, with objective performance metrics. That is measurement science, it is useful to every developer regardless of size, and it is the kind of work NIST does well. We would support expanding Sec. 123 and Sec. 122, the GAO review of regulatory impediments, with the resources currently proposed for CAISI.

## 5. The premise problem

We want to be direct about why we are asking for these deletions, because it is not cost alone.

The incident reporting and verification architecture in this draft is built on the assertion that frontier models may cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. That assertion is unfounded. No incident, no evaluation and no published result supports it. It has been advanced by a small and well-funded advocacy network, financed most prominently through Open Philanthropy and its successor vehicle, Coefficient Giving, whose grantmaking and lobbying have had outsized influence on Washington's AI policy debate. We do not impute motives to anyone. We are saying that a policy premise this thin should not be codified into a permanent federal reporting and audit regime with million-dollar-per-day penalties attached.

Congress does not need to adopt that premise to act on AI. Fraud is real, and Sec. 131 and Sec. 132 address it. Unauthorized access to systems is real, and it is already a crime, which is why Title III's work on model-weight security is worth doing. Worker disruption is real, and Title II addresses it. Every genuine problem in this draft has a provision attached to it that we can support, and every provision we oppose traces back to the one premise we cannot.

## 6. Comments on the introduced FRONTIER Act

The frontier-governance core of this discussion draft was introduced on July 23 as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act. Our comments apply to that bill with equal force, and we would add one more. We understand H.R. 9925 adds an exclusive federal authority to restrict the deployment of a frontier model on imminent-catastrophic-risk grounds, with penalties an order of magnitude above those in Sec. 111. That is the same unfounded premise with a deployment-blocking power attached to it, and we oppose it for the same reasons.

## Conclusion

ACIA's members want a federal AI framework. We want one national standard, permanently, that replaces the patchwork rather than repapering it in Washington. Strike Sec. 102, Sec. 111 and Sec. 112. Strike the definitions in Sec. 101 that give the doomsday vocabulary legal effect. Remove the sunset in Sec. 121. Keep the fraud, free speech, cybersecurity, testbed and workforce titles, which do real work, and put NIST's measurement scientists rather than a new safety bureaucracy at the center of the standards work.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on redline language, and we are glad to walk through the member cost data in aggregate. Thank you for the genuinely open process you have run, and for the bipartisan effort behind it.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

Enclosure: ACIA member compliance-cost survey, August 2026, aggregate results summary
